label: copy-phase input "s" (fed-back s, from 3rd copied token on)
explanation: Fires only in the copy phase when the fed-back input token is "s" (i.e. the model just emitted s), and only from recall_idx 2 onward (never at the delimiter or the first copy step; never in the original phase even when s is input). Every activation satisfies the predicate (recall 1.0); ~13% of qualifying s inputs are silent, often the last step or a repeated s. Strongest activations occur when s is the 3rd original token (recall_idx 2, step right after <DEL>+2); a second consecutive s fires noticeably weaker (~0.3-0.5 of the first). Does not fire on any other token or on out_tok s.

issues: The predicate itself holds up. On the test split it scores precision 0.868, recall 1.0, F1 0.929 and mass recall 1.0. misses --split test shows 0 missed activations, and the activations on fed-back s at recall_idx 1 are exactly 0 (16670 cases).

The label is off by one. At copy step recall_idx r the input is orig(r-1), so recall_idx >= 2 means the s is the 2nd copied token or later (orig(1) onward), not the 3rd. For example, 'q s 0 w <DEL> q [s]' fires with s as the 2nd copied token. The feature is silent only when s is the FIRST copied token.

The magnitude claim is false. The explanation says the strongest activations come at recall_idx 2. In fact recall_idx 2 is the weakest bucket: mass share 0.155, and only 7% of the top activation quartile, against 33% of the bottom quartile. The peak is at recall_idx 3, i.e. fed-back s = orig(2), the third original token. That bucket has mass share 0.33, covers 46% of the top quartile, and has precision 0.993. The top dev examples agree: 'q h [s:0.86]', 'a r [s:0.85]', '3 l [s:0.84]'.

The claim that silent s inputs are 'often at the last step' is overstated. Precision at to_go==0 is 0.818, compared with 0.868 overall, so silent cases are only slightly concentrated there. The false positives are spread fairly evenly: about 0.81 to 0.88 precision across prev_tok type (digit or letter), in_count, n_seen(s) and L. No systematic false-positive class turned up.

These claims do hold: activity is copy-phase only (no activations in the original or delimiter phases), the feature fires only on input s (in_tok lift 32x, every other token 0), out_tok is not the driver (about 2.1x for every value), and a repeated s fires more weakly (precision 0.72 when prev_tok is s, with the second s at about 0.3 to 0.5 of the first in the examples).

No better predicate is offered. Variants restricted by to_go or in_count lowered F1 (0.83 to 0.85), and the original predicate's F1 of 0.929 already reflects diffuse false positives rather than a gap that can be fixed.
